<reason>PRO built one sustained, escalating argument — that every example of "reform working" was actually a program ending, shrinking, or being struck down — and forced CON to keep conceding into it. By Rebuttal 2 and Closing, CON's own admissions (citizenship-by-investment is "small, already-dying," and reformed residency visas "converge" with ordinary entrepreneur channels) handed PRO the closing line that nothing distinctively "for sale" was left to defend. CON's best material — sovereignty, shadow-channel diversion, and the distinction between citizenship and residency instruments — was real and forced PRO to sharpen its case (which it did, distinguishing continuously-monitored ordinary channels from a single audited wire transfer), but CON never cleanly answered the specific pressure-question hypothetical of a lawfully-acquired passport later sanctioned: pointing to "the sanctions regime" doesn't resolve PRO's structural point that a purchased EU passport cannot be entry-banned from the Union the way a non-citizen can be, an externality unique to the sale that CON left standing. CON's closing reasserted that reform already delivered PRO's endpoint, but that argument concedes the revenue-generating property/passport-shortcut mechanism is gone, which is exactly what PRO needed. PRO's Rebuttal 1 was flagged as clipped for length, a real execution cost, but the substance before the cutoff had already made the key move.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's reform-equals-abolition squeeze (A2.3–A2.4, sharpened by the Q1 pressure question and crystallized in the Closing) was decisive: CON's own list of "successful reforms" (Cyprus shut, Malta struck down, Portugal's property route killed) matched exactly what the motion asks for, and CON never found a program that survived reform while still being a genuine "sale" rather than an ordinary investment/residence channel.</best_rebuttal>
